5 of 5 people found the following review helpful An honest, and at times amusing, look at the Afghanistan the media rarely show you By Steven W Palmer on January 9, 2014 Format: Kindle Edition Let me start off by saying I don't like these types of books. I find these 'behind the scenes, true life adventure' tales tend to be dryer than the Gobi desert at high noon. Invariably they are heavy on detail and light on any form of prosaic proficiency or artistic merit. So this was as refreshing as that first cold beer on a hot summer's day. Dave pulls no punches in his views and opinions of the inefficiencies and ineptitude of both the Coalition forces and the civilian contractors who often see such war zones as nothing more than lucrative cash cows, or indeed the Afghan security forces and politicians who seem to view corruption and pilfering as a perk of the job. His honesty in admitting his early blinkered Stars and Stripes idealism only endears the author to you more as continued infighting and negativity within the external authorities charged with 'bettering' the country as well as the often contradictory rules of the culture he's living within gradually make him realise that the mission to bring Afghanistan to peace and on a par with other developing countries is somewhat akin to a blind man attempting to ice skate up Everest while wrestling a rabid mongoose. The juxtaposition that he portrays throughout; of a country steeped in history and with sometimes cruel yet still beautiful landscapes, the ordinary people (both Afghan and within the armed forces and civilian organisations) who are truly trying to make a difference, against a background of struggle, resistance, descent into self destructive fundamentalism and a country plunged decades backwards from the cosmopolitan place it was 40 years ago gives the reader a totally different picture from anything that we have ever seen in the media. It's strange to call arrogance or cockiness endearing qualities, but, with Kaelin, that's exactly what they are, and it is these attributes that carried him (pretty successfully) through ten years in one of the world's most dangerous areas. From visits to a stadium still haunted by the echoing cries of the Taliban's victims to illicit visits to back street bordellos to walking paths trod by Alexander the Great, Dave takes you on a journey not only of the senses but one of learning. The mistakes and FUBARS made on this mission of rebuilding are all too obvious as Dave paints a picture of incompetency, greed, lack of empathy and a basic lack of caring that has made the whole exercise seem almost pointless. But as Dave points out; if he, or any of the foreign workers based there, manage to make even a small bit of difference then maybe, just maybe, that effect will ripple outwards and once the main coalition forces withdraw, there will be more people to stand against any resurgence of the Taliban. And despite the despondency reported in the media, and also despite the relentless rolling forward of an uncaring military-industrial complex, the book does have that message of hope at its heart. That maybe one day, Afghanistan will once more be a cosmopolitan country, free of the shackles of an insidious group who have twisted a religion for their own (and their Wahhabi masters) ends. I also have a feeling that should this book fall into the hands of the 'people at the top' there will be a lot of uncomfortable fidgeting in seats of power. A great read and an insightful and honest examination of one of the great dilemmas of the 21st Century.

I forsee a lot of "I don't, I sleep horribly" comments in this thread's future, so I'm going to post a giant list of tips for good sleep habits that I wrote up a couple months ago.

  • Consume as little caffeine as possible. If you're not used to it, a little will screw your system up entirely. If you are used to it, it can still cause issues that makes your sleep clock go haywire.

  • Exercise early or in the middle of the day. Exercise promotes healthy sleep along with all the other benefits it has. 20 or 30 minutes of running in the morning could mean falling asleep 30 minutes earlier at night, and the sleep will be much more refreshing in general. There is one caveat, though: don't exercise relatively soon before bed. Exercising before bed (3-4 hours at most) will essentially wake your body and mind up. It'll release all sorts of hormones that keep you alert, including adrenaline. This will make it a lot harder to fall asleep.

  • Stay away from electronics for at least a couple of hours before bed. The light from the screens, especially blue light, can cause your body to keep itself from producing melatonin, which is the main hormone you need to fall asleep. Programs like f.lux can help mitigate this if you have to use a screen, but it's best to avoid it altogether if possible.

  • Stay calm and relaxed. Easier said than done, I know, but if you stress yourself out about anything it can wake you up even more than you were in the first place. Practice meditation if that's your thing, or find some sort of creative outlet that helps reduce stress to do before bed. I find what works best for me is laying in bed and just daydreaming about whatever. I've had entire stories play out in my head while trying to fall asleep. If I start drifting towards something stressful, I just stop, acknowledge it, and reorient my thoughts back onto my story.

  • Don't use your bed for things other than sleep. If you do other things in your bed, your brain begins to disassociate your bed with sleep and start considering it just a place to do things. If you use your bed only for sleep, getting in bed will basically be telling your instinctual brain that it's time for sleep and it will start preparing itself.

  • Make a routine. This is the biggest one, I think, and it kind of plays on the same point as the last one. If you make a routine that you do every night before bed, whether it's reading a book, playing an instrument, or just turning off the lights and listening to music, your brain will associate that with sleep. Having a routine like that will mean that once you start the routine, your body starts preparing to go into sleep mode and by the time you get in bed you're already ready to fall asleep. This is a huge help, probably the best I've found.

  • If nothing else helps in the long term, I would suggest using melatonin supplements. Be VERY careful about using these, though. Melatonin supplements can be bought over the counter pretty much anywhere, in 5mg and 10mg tablets. What you would do is get a small dose, probably 1/2 of a 5mg tablet to start off, and take it 30 minutes before you go to bed for a few nights. What this will do is help your body realize when it needs to produce the hormone itself and help set your body's natural clock to where it needs to be. You need to be very careful about this though, as taking it too much will be terrible in the long run. If you take melatonin supplements every night for a long period of time, your body will start relying on it. You'll produce less and less of your own melatonin, until eventually falling asleep on your own is nearly impossible. You won't get tired as much, which sounds like a good thing, but even if you're not feeling tired you still need that sleep. It hinders everything you do. You could become irritable, you could become lethargic, it might even be hard for you to think straight if you let it go on too long. Fixing this can take years. I learned all of this the hard way.

  • If you get to this point and you're still having issues, see a doctor. Get an appointment with a sleep specialist and talk to them. Go in for a sleep study if needed. They'll help you get back on the right track, or at least as right of a track as you can get on if it's bad.

  • Use soothing noises like on MyNoise. This site has an insane amount of high quality background noises. I use it for everything. Sleeping, studying, meditation, etc.
  • If you don't have trouble falling asleep but wake up often or just don't feel rested (by waking up often and don't remember it the next day), maybe there is a medical indication like apnoe. Consider asking your doctor about it.
